query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered promising for high-heat wear-resistant use and is suitable for thin-film applications; because bulk preparation is expensive, applying it as a coating on a conventional metal is more practical. Earlier studies reported improved wear or mechanical performance from high-entropy-alloy coatings on Al, Ni, and titanium-alloy substrates, and simulations of FeNiCrCoCu on Cu indicated that sliding speed affects tangential and normal forces. Other work associated composition and grain size with changes in wear damage. However, most prior studies examined a limited operating regime or the properties of the alloys themselves rather than the overall wear resistance of coatings under varied thermal conditions. Subject to retaining FeNiCrCoCu as a coating on a Cu matrix, what single intervention could improve its overall wear resistance during sliding across varied thermal and contact regimes? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its causal mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to an unchanged coating in matched tests, the boundaries within which it should hold, supporting evidence from the introduction, and an experiment with a clear rejection criterion for both the predicted outcome and the proposed mechanism.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a refractory element, such as Ti, to the FeNiCrCoCu coating can improve its overall wear resistance during sliding across varied thermal and contact regimes.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu coating on a Cu matrix
generation.intervention: Addition of a refractory element, such as Ti
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a stable solid solution phase
generation.mechanism: The addition of Ti increases the hardness and wear resistance of the coating by forming a stable solid solution phase and potentially precipitating out hard phases.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu coating
generation.boundary: The improvement in wear resistance is expected to be most significant at high temperatures and under abrasive wear conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of Ti to be added and the optimal processing conditions to achieve the desired microstructure and properties are uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Sliding wear tests at varied temperatures and contact pressures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the wear rate of the Ti-added FeNiCrCoCu coating is not significantly lower than that of the unchanged coating, the hypothesis is falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [ [1] ], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years [ [2] ]. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co [ [3] ].

First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [ [4] , [5] ]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [6] ]. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [ [7] ] and yield strength σ 0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [ [5] ].
